title: Audio and music basics: waveforms to spectrograms

questions.q: In the lab described in the lesson, what is the calculated frequency resolution (width of each frequency bin) given a sample rate of 44100 Hz and a window size of 1024 samples?
questions.why: The lesson states that freq_resolution is calculated as sr / n_fft. With sr = 44100 and n_fft = 1024, the calculation is 44100 / 1024 ≈ 43.0664 Hz.

questions.q: According to the 'Under the hood' section, what is the purpose of multiplying a slice of the signal by a Hann window function before applying the DFT?
options: To increase the sample rate of the signal
To taper the edges to zero to avoid leakage where energy from one frequency bleeds into another
To convert the signal from the time domain to the frequency domain
To remove all high-frequency noise from the audio
questions.answer: To taper the edges to zero to avoid leakage where energy from one frequency bleeds into another
questions.why: The lesson explicitly states that the Hann window 'tapers the edges to zero to avoid "leakage" where energy from one frequency bleeds into another.'

questions.q: In the ComfyUI audio stack, which component is responsible for converting linear frequency magnitudes into the mel scale to mimic human hearing?
questions.why: The lesson states: 'The MelConverter in autoencoder.py is a critical piece. It converts linear frequency magnitudes into the mel scale, which mimics human hearing.'

questions.q: Based on the lab results, why did the peak frequency for the synthesized 440 Hz tone appear at 430.664 Hz instead of exactly 440 Hz?
options: The signal was corrupted by aliasing during synthesis.
The Hann window function distorted the frequency content.
The frequency resolution limits precision, so the peak falls in the nearest bin (bin 10).
The sample rate was too low to capture the 440 Hz frequency.
questions.answer: The frequency resolution limits precision, so the peak falls in the nearest bin (bin 10).
questions.why: The lesson explains that 440 / 43.0664 ≈ 10.21, so the peak falls in the 10th bin, which is 10 * 43.0664 = 430.664 Hz. This demonstrates the binning effect due to frequency resolution.

questions.q: What is the Nyquist limit for a signal sampled at 10 kHz, and what happens to frequencies above this limit?
questions.answer: The Nyquist limit is 5000 Hz (or 5 kHz). Any frequency above this limit will 'fold back' into a lower frequency, a phenomenon known as aliasing.
questions.why: The lesson defines the Nyquist limit as sr / 2. For a 10 kHz sample rate, this is 5000 Hz. It further states that 'Any frequency above this limit will appear as a fake frequency below it' due to aliasing.
